component.name: Flux Backup
component.summary: Fast snapshot backups of your files and your whole system

description.p: Flux Backup keeps snapshots of your folders on an external drive or an SSH server, on a schedule or when a drive is plugged in. Each snapshot shows everything as it was, and browsing, comparing and restoring take moments.
Choose how each profile stores its backups:

ul.li: Mirror: plain folders you can open with any file manager; unchanged files are hard links, so every snapshot is cheap
Vault: deduplicated across files and snapshots, compressed, and encrypted

description.p: Retention rules with a preview of what would be kept, restores that keep your current files, a file browser for every snapshot, backups of system files through an administrator password, and a full command-line tool (flux) for scripts and servers.

screenshot.caption: A profile's overview while a backup runs
Find a file in every snapshot, including files deleted since
See when the backup drive fills up
Recovering an existing backup on a new computer

description.p: Speed, and a Vault that heals from your files.

ul.li: Faster Vault backups: about a third of the processor time per piece stored, packs written while files are read, and photos, video and archives no longer compressed for nothing
New Vaults are encrypted with AES (XAES-256-GCM), about five times as fast; Vaults made before work as they did
Faster restores of large files, and faster pruning
Encryption on or off for a Vault, asked when it is set up and in its Settings
A new backup set up in three questions: what, where, and how it is stored
Repair: a damaged Vault takes off its list what it can no longer read, and the next backup stores it again from your files
Pruning never makes damage in a Vault permanent, and a copy of a backup no longer follows it into damage
A warning when the backup drive is slower than it should be (TRIM not reaching an SSD, a USB 3 drive on a USB 2 port)

description.p: A fix for starting at login, and a nudge to keep a Borg backup's key safe.

ul.li: An encrypted Borg backup whose key hasn't been exported says so on its Overview, with a button that exports the key to a folder you choose
Start at login no longer opens a blank "Could not connect to localhost" window

description.p: Getting files back, made to start where they were lost.

ul.li: Previous versions and Restore deleted files here in the right-click menu of Nautilus, Nemo and Dolphin, with Leave out of backups and Back up this folder beside them
Browse in Files: any snapshot, read-only, in the file manager
A recovery code that opens an encrypted backup when the password is lost
A Compact layout by default: a backup's Overview on one screen, a sidebar that folds to icons, a text size and the desktop's accent colour
A preview before restoring, and undo after deleting snapshots
Safe to unplug: the USB drive is unmounted and powered off when its backup ends
A warning when the backup drive is failing, and when a drive doesn't suit the backup
Notifications with buttons, quiet hours, and the time left wherever a backup or restore runs
Delete several snapshots at once, sizes next to every folder, and skipping what a project's .gitignore ignores
A calm weekly note when every backup is fine
New encrypted Vaults hide file sizes by default

description.p: A refinement release: what was there, made clearer, safer and quicker to use.

ul.li: Flux Sentry: unusual-change detection that learns how much of each backup normally changes, so a quiet backup warns early and a busy one doesn't cry wolf
Repair data for encrypted backups (Reed-Solomon parity): verifying every byte rebuilds what a failing drive has damaged
Restore tests sized by what a pass must prove: enough files to catch damage to 1% of them, 99% certain
Restore tests read files back and check them as they stream, without writing anything anywhere, so an encrypted backup stays encrypted while it's tested
Each backup's settings at a glance on its overview, and every backup's side by side in a sortable table
The recovery checklist has a button for each thing it asks: back up, keep the password elsewhere, export the Borg key, test a restore, add a place
A warning when a scheduled backup's password is set to be asked for each time, with a one-click fix
Statuses that agree everywhere, red only for what isn't protected, and a calmer overview
Times are typed the way you write them, on a 12- or 24-hour clock, and custom times show their next runs
Closing the window keeps Flux in the system tray (it can be turned off), and starting it again shows the running one
Man pages with examples for every command

description.p: The 1.0 release: backups you can recover anywhere, in formats that are written down and frozen.

ul.li: Recover an existing backup on a new computer, from the welcome screen: Flux finds it on a drive or server and sets it up again with its settings
A small program kept next to encrypted backups reads them without Flux, on any Linux
Export files from a snapshot as a .tar.zst or .zip archive, with checksums
Several places for one backup, including copies kept somewhere else
Restore tests on a schedule, and a warning when a backup shows ransomware-like changes
Notifications to a phone, a chat or a monitoring service through webhooks
Templates for new backups, a rule tester that says why a file is or isn't backed up, and a calendar of snapshots
Stronger password settings for encrypted backups, an optional unlock file, and sparse files kept sparse
Network rules: Wi-Fi networks and upload limits by time of day
Backups made by every earlier version are read and carried on

description.p: Easier, finer-grained restores, clearer setup, a way in from Back In Time, cron as a scheduler, and a new look in GNOME's own colours.

ul.li: Start a new backup from a Back In Time profile: folders, exclusions, schedule and what to keep come over, and its snapshots stay untouched
Restore single files from anywhere in a snapshot, and bring back just what was deleted in one click
Restore removed or changed files straight from the list of what changed
The file size limit takes a unit and warns when it would leave out almost everything
Comparing with your files explains what the size limit leaves out and hides folder-date noise
Setup explains in plain words what each backup does, and settings can go back to the recommended defaults
Scheduled backups can run with cron instead of systemd timers, and still catch up on missed ones
Backing up to a drive that isn't plugged in says so at once, instead of seeming to run forever
A new look in GNOME's own colours, with each backup's last 30 days drawn as bars

description.p: Backups that don't need Flux, an app that shows at a glance whether you're protected, and faster backups.

ul.li: A new look, and an All backups page that answers "am I protected right now?"
Setting up a backup is a step-by-step guide, and the password is chosen there, so scheduled backups never wait for one
Settings groups open in a dialog over the editor
Faster backups and browsing: Vault splits large files on every core, and spinning disks get large files two at a time
Compatibility mode: store backups with rsync or Borg in their own formats, with a recovery guide and script kept next to them
Export profiles to borgmatic, restic, rsync and Borg, and import Flux profiles
Find files across all snapshots, see every version of a file, open a copy, and preview a restore before it changes anything
A size estimate while setting up, and a forecast of when the backup drive fills up
Pause scheduled backups, skip them on metered connections, and monthly verification and weekly upkeep
Health warnings in words, a Preferences page, right-click menus, and settings without an advanced mode

description.p: First release: Mirror and Vault engines, local drives and SSH servers, systemd schedules, the desktop app, system backups, and read-only mounts of snapshots.
